analysis.one_liner: Requires two-person crews and stricter safety rules for trains carrying hazardous materials.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan Railway Safety Act of 2026 has received no hearing, markup, or vote since being referred to a House subcommittee three days after its introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would impose a package of safety rules on the largest freight railroads: a minimum two-person crew on most freight trains, speed caps for trains hauling flammable or toxic cargo, mandatory wayside defect detectors to catch overheated bearings and broken equipment, real-time sharing of what hazardous chemicals are on each train with first responders, safer tank cars, and civil penalties of up to $5 million for violations that cause death or serious injury. It would also fund emergency-response training and equipment for communities through fees on companies that ship hazardous materials. It is the House successor to the Railway Safety Act written after the 2023 East Palestine, Ohio derailment.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live along freight rail lines, especially near tracks used by trains carrying flammable liquids, toxic-by-inhalation chemicals, or explosives; rail workers who inspect and operate trains; and volunteer and local fire and emergency responders, who get training grants, protective equipment funding, and access to train chemical manifests they currently may not receive in real time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rail-line communities, rail workers, first responders

how_it_helps.text: Requires most Class I freight trains to operate with at least a two-person crew, with no exceptions for high-hazard trains or trains over 7,500 feet long [S2].
Caps all trains at 50 mph, and high-hazard flammable-liquid trains at 40 mph in high-threat urban areas unless they use the newest DOT-117-class tank cars [S2].

Requires Class I railroads to build networks of wayside defect detectors on busy main lines, including detectors positioned so any train is scanned within roughly 10-20 miles of entering a populated area, and to report data on detector failures [S2].

Requires railroads to generate real-time electronic train consist information and share it with fusion centers and, when responding to an incident, with first responders and law enforcement, and bars railroads from withholding it [S2].

Raises rail safety civil penalties to as much as $1 million per violation and up to $5 million when a violation causes death, serious illness, or severe injury, with penalties doubled for patterns of repeated violations [S2].
Bars any tank car not meeting DOT-117 or equivalent standards from carrying certain flammable liquids starting December 31, 2027, with a possible one-year delay [S2].
Bars railroads from limiting the time employees have to complete railcar, locomotive, and brake inspections, and requires qualified inspectors and periodic freight car inspections [S2].
Requires each railroad to maintain a toll-free hotline for reporting blocked highway-rail grade crossings, with the number posted publicly [S2].

Funds hazardous materials emergency response grants for states, tribes, and local responders, paid for by annual registration fees of $250-$5,000 on hazardous materials registrants, with 90% federal cost share for states and 100% for tribes, and creates a program to quickly reimburse communities hit by significant hazardous materials incidents [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The Class I freight railroads, which would bear the cost of two-person crews, speed restrictions, defect detector networks, safer tank cars, real-time data systems, and penalties up to $5 million per violation; chemical and hazardous-materials shippers, who would pay annual registration fees; and to the extent compliance costs are passed through, customers who ship freight by rail.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large freight railroads and hazmat shippers

drawbacks.text: The two-person crew requirement includes exceptions and a waiver process for some operations, so it would not mandate two-person crews everywhere; non-mainline track, helper locomotives, and operations already running with fewer than two people a year before enactment are exempted unless the Secretary finds they are unsafe [S2].

The provision on very long trains only directs the Transportation Secretary to review the safety concerns identified in a GAO report and update rules if the Secretary considers it necessary; if the Secretary does nothing, the bill only requires a report justifying the inaction [S2].

Chronically blocked grade crossings, a top local complaint, are addressed mainly with a $2 million National Academy of Sciences study due in two years and a hotline requirement, not with restrictions on how long trains can block a crossing [S2].

The costs of compliance — crews, detectors, tank car replacement by the end of 2027, and penalties up to $5 million — fall on the large railroads, and some of that cost is likely to be passed into freight shipping prices [S2].

New speed limits and crew rules can add operational friction to freight networks, which the bill acknowledges by requiring studies of network efficiency impacts of blocked-crossing fixes and directing regulators to comply with cost-benefit review under Executive Order 12866 [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety provisions target specific, documented failure modes — one-person crews on mile-plus trains, missed overheated bearings, missing chemical manifests at derailment scenes — and the costs land on a small group of highly profitable railroads and shippers rather than on households. The main honest caveats are that several headline complaints (long trains, blocked crossings) get studies and hotlines rather than binding rules, and the crew-size mandate is softened by exceptions and waivers. On balance the bill's benefits to communities and workers outweigh its costs, but it is less sweeping than its title suggests.

outcome.mechanism: The bill has sat in committee since March 2026: the House sent it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Science, Space, and Technology Committee on the day it was introduced, and three days later it was sent to the Railroads subcommittee, with no hearing, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Deluzio introduced the Railway Safety Act of 2026 on March 2, 2026, joined by Reps. LaLota, Garamendi, and Rulli as original cosponsors [S2].
The same day, the House referred the bill to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and, in addition, to the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology [S4].
On March 3, 2026, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials; the action history shows no further steps [S4].
The bill has 13 cosponsors, split 7 Republicans and 6 Democrats [S3].

Its predecessor, the Railway Safety Act of 2023 written after the East Palestine derailment, cleared a Senate committee in 2023 with bipartisan support but was never given floor votes in both chambers, leaving the safety provisions it contained unenacted (widely reported; not in the provided sources).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Class I freight railroads, which for now avoid the two-person crew requirement, speed limits, defect detector networks, tank car phase-out, and penalties of up to $5 million per violation that the bill would impose.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The big freight railroads, for now

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is genuinely bipartisan — 13 cosponsors split 7 Republicans and 6 Democrats, with original cosponsors from both parties — and no votes have occurred, so the partisan shape of any opposition is not yet visible in the record [S3].

industries.note: The bill targets the industry's cost-cutting model directly: two-person crews, 40-50 mph speed caps on hazard trains, defect detector networks spaced near populated areas, mandatory real-time chemical manifests for first responders, periodic freight car inspections, and penalties up to $5 million for violations causing death or serious injury. The predecessor bill's provisions were written in response to derailments like East Palestine, and the industry fought them.

industries.industry: Tank car manufacturers and retrofit shops
industries.note: The phase-out of non-DOT-117 tank cars for certain flammable liquids by December 31, 2027 (possibly extended to 2028) forces a fleet-wide replacement and retrofit effort, and the bill funds tank car safety research and a GAO study of North American manufacturing capacity.

Small railroads get lighter treatment: civil penalty caps of $200,000 (or $500,000 in death/injury cases) instead of $1 million-$5 million, a possible waiver from the toll-free blocked-crossing hotline, and exclusion of tourist and excursion operations from audits, while the crew-size mandate applies only to Class I railroads.

Annual registration fees of $250-$5,000 per registrant would fund the Hazardous Materials Emergency Preparedness Fund, a direct cost to companies that ship hazardous materials that pays for community emergency preparedness.

industries.industry: Emergency response training and equipment providers
industries.note: Grants to states, tribes, and local responders fund training (including virtual options), personal protective equipment purchases, and field exercises, with 90% federal cost share for states and 100% for tribes and protections ensuring funds flow to local entities.
A formula grant program helps commuter railroads that contract with Class I railroads pay for defect detection technology they would be required to install.

analysis.trajectory: Most House bills referred to subcommittee never reach a markup, and the near-identical Railway Safety Act of 2023 cleared a Senate committee in 2023 but never received floor votes in either chamber. Unless a high-profile derailment renews public pressure, this bill is likely to remain in subcommittee until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, dying without a vote despite its bipartisan sponsorship.
